cards.title: What is a **linear combination** of vectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$?
cards.body:
A vector of the form $c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2 + \dots + c_k v_k$, where $c_1, \dots, c_k$ are real numbers.

You scale each vector by its own number, then add the results. These two moves, scaling and adding, are the basic operations on vectors, and every other idea in linear algebra is built from them.

Example: $2\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix} - 3\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}$, so $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}$ is a linear combination of the two coordinate vectors.

Watch out: The numbers $c_i$ may be zero or negative. Taking all of them zero always gives the zero vector, so the zero vector is a linear combination of any list of vectors.
cards.searchQuery: linear combination of vectors definition

cards.title: What is the **span** of vectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$?
cards.body:
The set of all linear combinations $c_1 v_1 + \dots + c_k v_k$, with the $c_i$ ranging over all real numbers.

Key idea: The span is everything you can reach using only those vectors. One nonzero vector spans a line through the origin; two vectors that do not point along a common line span a plane through the origin.

Watch out: A span always contains the zero vector, so a line or plane that misses the origin is never the span of anything.
cards.searchQuery: span of vectors definition all linear combinations

cards.title: For nonzero $v, w \in \mathbb{R}^n$ at angle $\theta$, which formula gives $\cos\theta$ using the dot product and the lengths $\|v\|$, $\|w\|$?
cards.body:
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{v \cdot w}{\|v\|\,\|w\|}$

Here $v \cdot w = v_1 w_1 + \dots + v_n w_n$ is the **dot product**, and the **length** is $\|v\| = \sqrt{v \cdot v} = \sqrt{v_1^2 + \dots + v_n^2}$. A **unit vector** is a vector of length $1$; dividing any nonzero $v$ by $\|v\|$ gives the unit vector in its direction.

Why it matters: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ this formula is used as the definition of the angle, and in particular $v \cdot w = 0$ exactly when $\theta = 90^\circ$.

Watch out: The dot product of two vectors is a single number, not a vector.
cards.searchQuery: cosine of angle between vectors dot product formula

cards.title: State the **Cauchy–Schwarz inequality** for $v, w \in \mathbb{R}^n$, including when equality holds.
cards.body:
$|v \cdot w| \le \|v\|\,\|w\|$, with equality exactly when one of $v, w$ is a scalar multiple of the other.

Why it matters: It guarantees that the fraction $\dfrac{v \cdot w}{\|v\|\|w\|}$ lies in $[-1, 1]$, so it really is a cosine. It also gives the **triangle inequality** $\|v + w\| \le \|v\| + \|w\|$, because $\|v+w\|^2 = \|v\|^2 + 2\,v\cdot w + \|w\|^2 \le (\|v\| + \|w\|)^2$.

Key idea: For unit vectors $u, z$, expand $0 \le \|u - z\|^2 = 2 - 2\,u \cdot z$ and $0 \le \|u + z\|^2 = 2 + 2\,u \cdot z$. Together they give $|u \cdot z| \le 1$. Rescaling gives the general case.
cards.searchQuery: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality dot product equality condition

cards.title: Let $u = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $w = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Describe $\operatorname{span}\{u, w\}$ geometrically, and decide whether $b = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ lies in it.
cards.body:
The span is a plane through the origin, namely $z = x + y$, and $b$ lies in it because $b = 1\cdot u + 2\cdot w$.

Every combination has the form $a u + c w = (a, c, a + c)$, so its third entry equals the sum of the first two. That is exactly the plane $z = x + y$.

Check: $b = (1, 2, 3)$ has $3 = 1 + 2$, and $1\cdot(1,0,1) + 2\cdot(0,1,1) = (1, 2, 3)$.

Watch out: The vector $(1, 2, 4)$ is not in the span, since $4 \ne 1 + 2$. Whether a given vector is in a span is a question about solving equations for the coefficients.
cards.searchQuery: span of two vectors in R3 plane membership example

cards.title: Find $\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $v = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $w = \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Type it as an exact value.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

1. $v \cdot w = 2 - 1 + 2 = 3$.
2. $\|v\| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$ and $\|w\| = \sqrt{3}$.
3. $\cos\theta = \dfrac{3}{3\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

Check: $\|v\| = 3$ means $\tfrac13 v = (\tfrac23, -\tfrac13, \tfrac23)$ is the unit vector along $v$. It has dot product $1$ with $w$, and dividing by $\|w\| = \sqrt{3}$ gives the same cosine.
cards.searchQuery: cosine angle between two vectors in R3 computation

cards.title: Why is it false that any two nonzero vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ span a plane?
cards.body:
If one vector is a scalar multiple of the other, their span is only a line through the origin.

Example: $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-4\\-6\end{pmatrix}$ are both nonzero, but every combination $a\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix} + c\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-4\\-6\end{pmatrix} = (a - 2c)\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ lies on the same line.

Key idea: A plane needs two vectors that point in genuinely different directions. Later in this module that idea gets a precise name and a test.

Tip: Before trusting a count of vectors, ask whether any of them is already a combination of the others. If so, it adds nothing new to the span.
cards.searchQuery: two nonzero vectors span line not plane parallel

cards.title: Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix with columns $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and let $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$. How does the **column picture** define the **matrix–vector product** $Ax$?
cards.body:
$Ax = x_1 a_1 + x_2 a_2 + \dots + x_n a_n$, a linear combination of the columns of $A$ with the entries of $x$ as the weights.

So $Ax$ always lies in the span of the columns, and solving $Ax = b$ means asking whether $b$ is a combination of the columns and which weights make it so.

The **row picture** gives the same vector entry by entry: the $i$th entry of $Ax$ is (row $i$ of $A$) $\cdot\, x$.

Example: $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\3 & 4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix} = 2\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix} - 1\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\2\end{pmatrix}$. By rows: $1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot(-1) = 0$ and $3 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot (-1) = 2$.
cards.searchQuery: matrix vector product column picture combination of columns

cards.title: In Gaussian elimination, what is a **pivot**?
cards.body:
The nonzero entry in the current row and column that is used to clear the entries below it.

Elimination works down the diagonal. At step $k$ the pivot is the entry in position $(k, k)$ after earlier steps; its row is subtracted, in suitable multiples, from the rows below.

Key idea: The multiplier for a lower row is (the entry to be cleared) divided by the pivot, which is why a pivot must not be zero.

Watch out: The pivot is a number in the current, partly reduced matrix, not an entry of the original $A$ (except for the first one).
cards.searchQuery: pivot gaussian elimination definition nonzero entry

cards.title: What does **Gaussian elimination** do to a square system $Ax = b$, and what does it produce?
cards.body:
It subtracts multiples of earlier rows from later rows to create zeros below each pivot, turning the system into an upper-triangular system $Ux = c$ that is solved from the bottom up.

Upper triangular means every entry below the diagonal is $0$. The last equation then has one unknown, the one above it two, and so on: this bottom-up solving is **back-substitution**.

Why it works: Subtracting a multiple of one equation from another can be undone by adding it back, so the new system has exactly the same solutions as the old one. Apply every step to $b$ as well as to $A$.

Tip: Keep $b$ as an extra column next to $A$ so each row operation is done once, on the whole row.
cards.searchQuery: gaussian elimination upper triangular back substitution

cards.title: For an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, which matrix $E_{ij}$ subtracts $\ell$ times row $j$ from row $i$ (with $i > j$), and how is it applied?
cards.body:
$E_{ij}$ is the identity matrix with $-\ell$ in row $i$, column $j$; the step is the product $E_{ij}A$, with $E_{ij}$ on the left.

This is the **elimination matrix** for one step. For $3 \times 3$ and $i = 2$, $j = 1$, $\ell = 2$:

$$E_{21} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\-2 & 1 & 0\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$$

Row 2 of $E_{21}A$ is $(-2)\cdot$(row 1) $+ 1\cdot$(row 2) $+ 0\cdot$(row 3), which is row 2 minus $2$ times row 1. Rows 1 and 3 are unchanged.

Watch out: Multiplying on the left changes rows; multiplying on the right, $AE$, would combine columns instead. The inverse of $E_{ij}$ puts $+\ell$ in the same place, because it adds the multiple back.
cards.searchQuery: elimination matrix subtract multiple of row identity

cards.title: For the system $2x - y = 0$, $-x + 2y = 3$, describe the row picture and the column picture and give the solution.
cards.body:
The solution is $(x, y) = (1, 2)$: the two lines meet there (row picture), and $b = \begin{pmatrix}0\\3\end{pmatrix}$ equals $1\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix} + 2\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ (column picture).

Row picture: each equation is a line in the plane, and the solution is their intersection point. Here $2(1) - 2 = 0$ and $-1 + 2(2) = 3$.

Column picture: write the system as $x\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix} + y\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\3\end{pmatrix}$. The question becomes which combination of the two columns produces $b$: one copy of the first column plus two of the second.

Key idea: Same system, same answer, two ways of seeing it. The column picture is the one that generalizes to column spaces later.
cards.searchQuery: row picture column picture 2x2 linear system example

cards.title: Solve by elimination: $x + y + z = 6$, $2x + 3y + 4z = 20$, $3x + 5y + 8z = 37$. Give the pivots and the solution.
cards.body:
The pivots are $1, 1, 1$ and the solution is $(x, y, z) = (1, 2, 3)$.

1. Subtract $2\times$ row 1 from row 2 and $3\times$ row 1 from row 3: $y + 2z = 8$ and $2y + 5z = 19$.
2. Subtract $2\times$ the new row 2 from row 3: $z = 3$.
3. Back-substitute: $y = 8 - 2(3) = 2$, then $x = 6 - 2 - 3 = 1$.

Check: $2(1) + 3(2) + 4(3) = 20$ and $3(1) + 5(2) + 8(3) = 37$.
cards.searchQuery: solve 3x3 linear system gaussian elimination pivots

cards.title: The system $x + 2y = 4$, $3x + cy = 12$ has a number $c$ for which elimination cannot produce two pivots. Find $c$ and say how many solutions the system then has.
cards.body:
$c = 6$: the second equation becomes $0 = 0$, so only one pivot appears and there are infinitely many solutions.

Subtract $3\times$ row 1 from row 2: the second equation becomes $(c - 6)\,y = 0$. If $c \ne 6$, the pivot $c - 6$ exists and gives $y = 0$, $x = 4$.

At $c = 6$ the second equation is just $3$ times the first ($3x + 6y = 12$), so every point of the line $x + 2y = 4$ is a solution. This is the **singular** case: fewer pivots than unknowns.

Watch out: If the right side were $3x + 6y = 13$ instead, the same elimination would give $0 = 1$ and no solution. A missing pivot allows two outcomes, depending on $b$.
cards.searchQuery: singular system missing pivot infinitely many solutions parameter

cards.title: Solve $2y + z = 7$, $x + y + 2z = 9$, $2x + y + z = 7$ by elimination. The first pivot position holds $0$, so first swap two rows (a **row exchange**).
cards.body:
$(x, y, z) = (1, 2, 3)$, found after exchanging rows 1 and 2; the pivots are $1, 2, -\tfrac52$.

1. Swap rows 1 and 2 so the first equation is $x + y + 2z = 9$ and the second is $2y + z = 7$.
2. Subtract $2\times$ row 1 from row 3: $-y - 3z = -11$.
3. Add $\tfrac12\times$ row 2 to row 3: $-\tfrac52 z = -\tfrac{15}{2}$, so $z = 3$.
4. Back-substitute: $y = (7 - 3)/2 = 2$ and $x = 9 - 2 - 6 = 1$.

Check: $2(2) + 3 = 7$ and $2(1) + 2 + 3 = 7$.
cards.searchQuery: row exchange zero pivot elimination solve system

cards.title: Why is it false that a $0$ in a pivot position means the system has no solution?
cards.body:
A zero pivot is often fixable by a row exchange; only when no lower row can supply a nonzero entry in that column is the system truly stuck.

Example: In $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 2\\3 & 4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\11\end{pmatrix}$, the first pivot position holds $0$. Swapping the rows gives $3x + 4y = 11$, $2y = 2$, so $y = 1$, $x = 7/3$. The system has a unique solution.

Key idea: When elimination cannot continue even after exchanging rows, the matrix is singular, and then the system has either no solution or infinitely many, depending on $b$.

Watch out: Not every zero encountered is a failure: a zero below a pivot is exactly what elimination is trying to create.
cards.searchQuery: zero pivot row exchange system still solvable

cards.title: How is the **matrix product** $AB$ defined when $A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $n \times p$?
cards.body:
$AB$ is the $m \times p$ matrix with entries $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{ik} b_{kj}$, the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ with column $j$ of $B$.

The same product can be seen in four ways:
- entry by entry: (row $i$ of $A$) $\cdot$ (column $j$ of $B$)
- by columns: column $j$ of $AB$ is $A$ times column $j$ of $B$
- by rows: row $i$ of $AB$ is row $i$ of $A$ times $B$
- as a sum of (column $k$ of $A$)(row $k$ of $B$) over $k$, each a column times a row

Watch out: The inner sizes must match: the number of columns of $A$ equals the number of rows of $B$.
cards.searchQuery: matrix product definition four ways rows columns

cards.title: Why is it false that $AB = BA$ for square matrices $A$ and $B$ of the same size?
cards.body:
Matrix multiplication is not commutative: in general $AB \ne BA$, and a single example shows it.

Example: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ we get $AB = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ but $BA = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$.

Why: $AB$ means "apply $B$ first, then $A$" to a vector, and the order in which two linear steps are done usually matters.

Watch out: This kills the formulas that rely on commuting. For instance $(A + B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2$, which is not $A^2 + 2AB + B^2$ in general. Multiplication is still associative, $(AB)C = A(BC)$.
cards.searchQuery: matrix multiplication not commutative AB not equal BA

cards.title: What is the **inverse matrix** of a square matrix $A$, and when does it exist?
cards.body:
A matrix $A^{-1}$ with $A A^{-1} = I$ and $A^{-1} A = I$; it exists exactly when elimination on $A$ (row exchanges allowed) produces $n$ pivots.

If $A^{-1}$ exists, $Ax = b$ has the unique solution $x = A^{-1} b$. A matrix with no inverse is called singular.

Tip: For square matrices, $AB = I$ alone already forces $BA = I$, so one product check is enough.

Watch out: In practice one solves $Ax = b$ by elimination and does not compute $A^{-1}$ first, which costs more.
cards.searchQuery: inverse matrix definition exists n pivots

cards.title: Use **Gauss–Jordan elimination** on $[A \mid I]$ to find the inverse of $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 3\\2 & 7\end{pmatrix}$.
cards.body:
$A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}7 & -3\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$

Gauss–Jordan elimination row-reduces the block matrix $[A \mid I]$ until the left half is $I$; the right half is then $A^{-1}$.

1. Subtract $2\times$ row 1 from row 2: $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 3\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ on the left, $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ on the right.
2. Subtract $3\times$ row 2 from row 1: the left becomes $I$ and the right becomes $\begin{pmatrix}7 & -3\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.

Why it works: Each row operation is multiplication by an invertible matrix $E$. The operations turn $A$ into $I$, so $EA = I$, and $E = E I$ is exactly what appears on the right.

Check: Row 1 of $A$ times the columns of the answer: $1\cdot7 + 3\cdot(-2) = 1$ and $1\cdot(-3) + 3\cdot1 = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: Gauss-Jordan elimination inverse matrix augmented identity

cards.title: What is the inverse of a product $AB$ of invertible $n \times n$ matrices?
cards.body:
$(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}$: the inverses in reverse order.

Why: $(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1}) = A (B B^{-1}) A^{-1} = A A^{-1} = I$. The same cancellation from the other side gives $(B^{-1}A^{-1})(AB) = I$.

Mnemonic: Socks and shoes. You put on socks, then shoes; to undo it you take off the shoes first, then the socks.

Watch out: $(AB)^{-1}$ is not $A^{-1}B^{-1}$ in general, since matrices do not commute. The product $AB$ is also invertible only if both $A$ and $B$ are.
cards.searchQuery: inverse of product of matrices reverse order

cards.title: For matrices $A$ and $B$ whose product $AB$ is defined, what is $(AB)^T$? (The **transpose** $A^T$ has entries $(A^T)_{ij} = A_{ji}$.)
cards.body:
$(AB)^T = B^T A^T$

Transposing swaps rows and columns, so $A^T$ is $A$ flipped across its diagonal. A **symmetric matrix** is one with $A^T = A$.

Why: The entry $(i, j)$ of $(AB)^T$ is the entry $(j, i)$ of $AB$, which is (row $j$ of $A$) $\cdot$ (column $i$ of $B$). That is also (row $i$ of $B^T$) $\cdot$ (column $j$ of $A^T$), the $(i, j)$ entry of $B^T A^T$.

Example: For any matrix $R$, the product $R^T R$ is symmetric, since $(R^T R)^T = R^T (R^T)^T = R^T R$.
cards.searchQuery: transpose of product B transpose A transpose symmetric

cards.title: If elimination on $A$ needs no row exchanges, what is the **LU factorization** of $A$ and what do the entries of $L$ record?
cards.body:
$A = LU$, with $U$ the upper-triangular result of elimination and $L$ lower triangular with $1$s on the diagonal and the elimination multipliers below it.

The entry $\ell_{ij}$ of $L$ is the multiplier used to clear position $(i, j)$. If row exchanges are needed, a permutation matrix $P$ (the identity with its rows reordered) fixes it: $PA = LU$.

Why: Elimination is $E_{32}E_{31}E_{21}A = U$, so $A = E_{21}^{-1}E_{31}^{-1}E_{32}^{-1}U$. In this order the multipliers drop into $L$ without mixing.

Why it matters: Solve $Ax = b$ in two cheap triangular steps, $Lc = b$ (forward) and then $Ux = c$ (back-substitution). The same $L$ and $U$ serve every new $b$.
cards.searchQuery: LU factorization A=LU multipliers lower triangular

cards.title: Factor $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 1\\2 & 5 & 4\\-1 & 1 & 8\end{pmatrix}$ as $LU$ and use it to solve $Ax = \begin{pmatrix}6\\16\\9\end{pmatrix}$.
cards.body:
$L = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\2 & 1 & 0\\-1 & 3 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $U = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 1\\0 & 1 & 2\\0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}$, and $x = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

1. Clear column 1: subtract $2\times$ row 1 from row 2 and add $1\times$ row 1 to row 3. The multipliers are $\ell_{21} = 2$ and $\ell_{31} = -1$. The rows are now $(0,1,2)$ and $(0,3,9)$.
2. Clear column 2: subtract $3\times$ row 2 from row 3, so $\ell_{32} = 3$ and the last row is $(0,0,3)$. This gives $U$.
3. Forward: $Lc = \begin{pmatrix}6\\16\\9\end{pmatrix}$ gives $c_1 = 6$, $c_2 = 16 - 12 = 4$, $c_3 = 9 + 6 - 12 = 3$.
4. Back: $Ux = c$ gives $z = 1$, $y = 4 - 2 = 2$, $x = 6 - 4 - 1 = 1$.

Check: The first row of $LU$ is $(1,2,1)$, and row 3 is $-1\cdot(1,2,1) + 3\cdot(0,1,2) + (0,0,3) = (-1, 1, 8)$.
cards.searchQuery: LU factorization example solve system forward back substitution

cards.title: A **permutation matrix** is the identity matrix with its rows in a different order. For $P = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 & 0\\0 & 0 & 1\\1 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, find $P^{-1}$ and say what $P$ does to $x = (x_1, x_2, x_3)$.
cards.body:
$P^{-1} = P^T = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 0 & 1\\1 & 0 & 0\\0 & 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, and $Px = (x_2, x_3, x_1)$.

The rows of $P$ are $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,1)$, $(1,0,0)$, so the entries of $Px$ are $x_2$, $x_3$, $x_1$: the entries cycle one place up. Undoing a cycle means cycling back, which is what $P^T$ does.

Why: The columns of a permutation matrix are also the columns of $I$ in some order, so different columns have dot product $0$ and each column has length $1$. That gives $P^T P = I$, hence $P^{-1} = P^T$.

Check: Three cycles return everything to its place, so $P^3 = I$, and $P^{-1} = P^2$ agrees with the matrix above.
cards.searchQuery: permutation matrix inverse transpose cyclic

cards.title: What is a **vector space**, and what is the one property that matters most in practice?
cards.body:
A set of objects that can be added and scaled by real numbers, following the usual rules, so that every linear combination of members stays in the set.

The usual rules are the ones you know from $\mathbb{R}^n$: addition is commutative and associative, there is a zero vector, every vector has an opposite, and scaling distributes over addition. Besides $\mathbb{R}^n$, the set of all $2 \times 2$ matrices is a vector space, with matrices as the "vectors".

Key idea: Closure. Adding two members, or scaling one, never leaves the set. This is exactly what you check for subspaces.

Watch out: A vector space can never be empty. It contains $0$, because $0 \cdot v = 0$ for any member $v$.
cards.searchQuery: vector space definition closure addition scalar multiplication

cards.title: What conditions make a subset $S$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ a **subspace**?
cards.body:
$S$ contains the zero vector, and for all $u, v \in S$ and every real $c$: $u + v \in S$ and $c\,u \in S$.

Equivalently, $S$ is nonempty and every linear combination of members of $S$ is again in $S$. A subspace is itself a vector space, sitting inside a bigger one.

Example: In $\mathbb{R}^3$ the subspaces are the origin alone, the lines through the origin, the planes through the origin, and $\mathbb{R}^3$ itself.

Tip: To disprove a subspace claim, check $0 \in S$ first. If the zero vector is missing, you are done.
cards.searchQuery: subspace definition conditions closed under addition scaling

cards.title: Give a subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that contains $0$ and is closed under scaling but is not a subspace.
cards.body:
The union of the two coordinate axes, $S = \{(x, y) : x = 0 \text{ or } y = 0\}$.

It contains $0$, and scaling a vector on an axis keeps it on that axis. But $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ are in $S$ while their sum $(1, 1)$ is not, so $S$ is not closed under addition.

Key idea: A union of two subspaces is generally not a subspace; closure under addition is the condition that fails.

Watch out: The first quadrant $\{(x,y) : x \ge 0, y \ge 0\}$ fails the other way: it is closed under addition but not under scaling by $-1$.
cards.searchQuery: union of two lines not a subspace counterexample

cards.title: What is the **column space** $C(A)$ of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, and what does it say about $Ax = b$?
cards.body:
$C(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A$: all vectors $Ax$. It is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$, and $Ax = b$ is solvable exactly when $b \in C(A)$.

This follows from the column picture: $Ax$ is a combination of the columns, so $b$ can be written as $Ax$ for some $x$ precisely when $b$ is a combination of the columns.

Watch out: The column space lives in $\mathbb{R}^m$ (the number of rows), not $\mathbb{R}^n$. A $3 \times 2$ matrix has a column space inside $\mathbb{R}^3$, and it cannot fill $\mathbb{R}^3$ with only two columns.
cards.searchQuery: column space definition span of columns Ax=b solvable

cards.title: What is the **null space** $N(A)$ of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, and why is it a subspace?
cards.body:
$N(A) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : Ax = 0\}$, the set of all solutions of $Ax = 0$; it is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Why: $0$ is a solution, and if $Ax = 0$ and $Ay = 0$ then $A(cx + dy) = c\,Ax + d\,Ay = 0$, so combinations of solutions are solutions.

Watch out: The solutions of $Ax = b$ with $b \ne 0$ do not form a subspace, since $x = 0$ is not among them. They are a shifted copy of $N(A)$, as the next unit shows.
cards.searchQuery: null space definition solutions Ax=0 subspace

cards.title: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 1\\0 & 0 & 1 & 3\\2 & 4 & 1 & 5\end{pmatrix}$, find the reduced row echelon form, the free variables and the special solutions of $Ax = 0$.
cards.body:
The reduced row echelon form is $R = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 1\\0 & 0 & 1 & 3\\0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$; the free variables are $x_2, x_4$, and the special solutions are $(-2, 1, 0, 0)$ and $(-1, 0, -3, 1)$.

**Reduced row echelon form** (RREF) has each pivot equal to $1$ with zeros above and below it, pivots moving right as you go down, and zero rows at the bottom. Here row 3 minus twice row 1 is $(0,0,1,3)$, which duplicates row 2 and cancels. The pivots are in columns 1 and 3.

A **free variable** belongs to a column without a pivot: $x_2$ and $x_4$ can be chosen freely. A **special solution** sets one free variable to $1$ and the others to $0$, then solves for the pivot variables. From $x_1 + 2x_2 + x_4 = 0$ and $x_3 + 3x_4 = 0$: $x_2 = 1$ gives $x_1 = -2$; $x_4 = 1$ gives $x_1 = -1$, $x_3 = -3$.

Key idea: $N(A)$ is the span of the special solutions.

cards.title: Describe $N(A)$ geometrically for $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 1\\2 & 4 & 3\\3 & 6 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
cards.body:
$N(A)$ is the line through the origin spanned by $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$.

1. Row 2 minus $2\times$ row 1 gives $(0,0,1)$, and row 3 minus $3\times$ row 1 gives $(0,0,1)$. Subtracting row 2 from the new row 3 leaves zeros.
2. The reduced form is $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 0\\0 & 0 & 1\\0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. Pivots are in columns 1 and 3, so $x_2$ is the only free variable.
3. Setting $x_2 = 1$ gives $x_1 = -2$ and $x_3 = 0$.

Check: $A\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} = -2\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix} + 1\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\\6\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$.

Watch out: Columns 1 and 2 are parallel, which is what the free variable $x_2$ detects: $2\times$(column 1) $-$ (column 2) $= 0$.

cards.title: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & 2\\2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$, which vectors $b = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$ make $Ax = b$ solvable?
cards.body:
Exactly those with $b_3 = b_1 + b_2$: the column space is a plane through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

1. Subtract row 1 from row 2 and $2\times$ row 1 from row 3 on the augmented matrix: the rows become $(1, 1 \mid b_1)$, $(0, 1 \mid b_2 - b_1)$, $(0, 1 \mid b_3 - 2b_1)$.
2. Subtract the new row 2 from row 3: the last row is $(0, 0 \mid b_3 - b_1 - b_2)$.
3. That row reads $0 = b_3 - b_1 - b_2$, so a solution exists exactly when the right side vanishes.

Check: Both columns satisfy it: $(1,1,2)$ has $2 = 1 + 1$ and $(1,2,3)$ has $3 = 1 + 2$. Two columns can span at most a plane inside $\mathbb{R}^3$.

cards.title: What is the **rank** of a matrix $A$?
cards.body:
The number of pivots that elimination finds in $A$; it is written $r$, and $r \le \min(m, n)$ for an $m \times n$ matrix.

Rank measures how many truly different directions the columns (and rows) carry. A system $Ax = b$ with $n$ unknowns has a unique solution, when it has one, exactly when $r = n$.

Watch out: Count pivots after elimination. The number of nonzero entries of $A$ says nothing about rank: the matrix with every entry equal to $1$ has rank $1$ however large it is.

cards.title: When are vectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ **linearly independent**?
cards.body:
When the only combination $c_1 v_1 + \dots + c_k v_k = 0$ is the one with every $c_i = 0$.

If some other combination gives $0$, the vectors are dependent: at least one of them is a combination of the others. Put the vectors as columns of a matrix $A$: they are independent exactly when $N(A) = \{0\}$, that is, when no column is free.

Example: $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\end{pmatrix}$ are dependent, since $2\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}2\\4\end{pmatrix} = 0$. $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ are independent.

Watch out: Any list containing the zero vector is dependent, since $1\cdot 0 = 0$ is a nontrivial combination.

cards.title: What is a **basis** of a subspace $V$, and what is the **dimension** of $V$?
cards.body:
A basis is a list of independent vectors that span $V$; the dimension of $V$ is the number of vectors in a basis, the same for every basis.

Every vector of $V$ is then a combination of the basis vectors in exactly one way. For $\mathbb{R}^n$ the standard basis (columns of $I$) has $n$ vectors, so $\dim \mathbb{R}^n = n$.

Example: A line through the origin has dimension $1$ and any nonzero vector on it is a basis. The columns of an $n \times n$ matrix form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ exactly when the matrix is invertible.

Watch out: Bases are not unique, but their size is. Never say "the" basis unless one has been fixed.
cards.searchQuery: basis and dimension of a subspace definition

cards.title: State the **rank–nullity theorem** for an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ of rank $r$.
cards.body:
$\dim N(A) = n - r$, equivalently $\dim C(A) + \dim N(A) = n$.

Why: Each of the $n$ columns is either a pivot column ($r$ of them) or a free column ($n - r$ of them). The special solutions, one per free variable, are independent and span $N(A)$, so they are a basis of $N(A)$ with $n - r$ vectors.

Why it matters: It makes counting possible. A $5 \times 8$ matrix has $n - r \ge 3$, so $Ax = 0$ always has nonzero solutions, no matter the entries.

Watch out: The $n$ here is the number of columns (unknowns), not the number of rows.

cards.title: For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ of rank $r$, what are the dimensions of $C(A)$, the row space $C(A^T)$, $N(A)$ and the left null space $N(A^T)$, and where does each live?
cards.body:
$C(A)$ and $C(A^T)$ both have dimension $r$ (in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$); $N(A)$ has dimension $n - r$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$; $N(A^T)$ has dimension $m - r$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$.

The **row space** $C(A^T)$ is the span of the rows of $A$. The **left null space** $N(A^T)$ is the set of $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with $A^T y = 0$, equivalently $y^T A = 0$: combinations of the rows that cancel to zero.

Key idea: Row operations do not change the row space, and the nonzero rows of the reduced form are $r$ independent rows, so the row space has dimension $r$, the same as the column space. Applying rank–nullity to $A^T$ gives $m - r$.

Tip: The two spaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ have dimensions adding to $n$, and the two in $\mathbb{R}^m$ add to $m$.

cards.title: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 1\\0 & 0 & 1 & 3\\2 & 4 & 1 & 5\end{pmatrix}$, give a basis for each of its four fundamental subspaces.
cards.body:
Rank $r = 2$. $C(A)$: $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Row space: $(1,2,0,1), (0,0,1,3)$. $N(A)$: $(-2,1,0,0), (-1,0,-3,1)$. $N(A^T)$: $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

- Pivots are in columns 1 and 3 of the reduced form, so columns 1 and 3 of $A$ itself are a basis of $C(A)$.
- The nonzero rows of the reduced form $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 1\\0 & 0 & 1 & 3\\0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ are a basis of the row space.
- The special solutions are a basis of $N(A)$, and $2 = 4 - 2$ of them.
- Row 3 minus twice row 1 minus row 2 is zero, so $y = (-2,-1,1)$ satisfies $y^T A = 0$, giving $N(A^T)$ with dimension $1 = 3 - 2$.

Watch out: Take the pivot columns from the original $A$, not from the reduced form, whose columns span a different space.

cards.title: How can you describe the complete set of solutions of $Ax = b$ when at least one solution exists?
cards.body:
Every solution is $x = x_p + x_n$, where $x_p$ is any one particular solution and $x_n$ ranges over all of $N(A)$.

Why: If $Ax_p = b$ and $Ax = b$, then $A(x - x_p) = 0$, so $x - x_p \in N(A)$. Conversely, adding any $x_n \in N(A)$ to $x_p$ leaves $Ax$ equal to $b$.

Key idea: The solution set is a shifted copy of the null space, a line, plane and so on, that misses the origin when $b \ne 0$. It is a single point when $N(A) = \{0\}$, that is when $r = n$.

Tip: Find $x_p$ by setting every free variable to $0$ and solving for the pivot variables.

cards.title: Are $v_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}$, $v_2 = \begin{pmatrix}2\\5\\7\end{pmatrix}$, $v_3 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}$ linearly independent? If not, give a nontrivial combination equal to $0$.
cards.body:
No: $v_1 - v_2 + v_3 = 0$.

Put the vectors as columns of $A$ and eliminate. Subtract $2\times$ row 1 from row 2 and $3\times$ row 1 from row 3: the rows become $(1,2,1)$, $(0,1,1)$, $(0,1,1)$. Row 3 minus row 2 is $0$, so only two pivots appear and column 3 is free.

Setting the free variable $c_3 = 1$: from $c_2 + c_3 = 0$ we get $c_2 = -1$, and from $c_1 + 2c_2 + c_3 = 0$ we get $c_1 = 1$.

Check: $(1 - 2 + 1,\ 2 - 5 + 3,\ 3 - 7 + 4) = (0, 0, 0)$.

cards.title: Find all solutions of $Ax = b$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 0\\0 & 1 & 1\\1 & 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $b = \begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\5\end{pmatrix}$.
cards.body:
$x = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\0\end{pmatrix} + t\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ for any real $t$: a line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ not through the origin.

1. Subtract row 1 from row 3: the rows are $(1,1,0 \mid 2)$, $(0,1,1 \mid 3)$, $(0,1,1 \mid 3)$. The last row minus the second is $0 = 0$, so $r = 2$ and $z$ is free.
2. Particular solution: $z = 0$ gives $y = 3$ and $x = -1$.
3. Null space: set $b = 0$ and $z = 1$, so $y = -1$ and $x = 1$.

Check: $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $A\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\5\end{pmatrix}$. The system is solvable because row 3 of $A$ is the sum of rows 1 and 2, and $b_3 = 5 = 2 + 3$.

cards.title: Why is it false that row operations never change the column space of a matrix?
cards.body:
Row operations preserve the row space and the null space but can change the column space.

Example: $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has column space spanned by $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. One row operation gives $R = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, whose column space is spanned by $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$. These are different lines.

Why: A row operation is multiplication on the left by an invertible matrix $E$, and $EA$ has different columns from $A$. But $Ax = 0$ exactly when $EAx = 0$, so the null space is the same, and the rows of $EA$ are combinations of the rows of $A$ and vice versa.

Tip: The pivot positions found in the reduced form still tell you which columns of the original $A$ are independent, so use those original columns for a basis of $C(A)$.

cards.title: What is the **orthogonal complement** $V^\perp$ of a subspace $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$?
cards.body:
$V^\perp = \{ w \in \mathbb{R}^n : w \cdot v = 0 \text{ for every } v \in V \}$, all vectors orthogonal to every vector of $V$.

$V^\perp$ is itself a subspace, and $\dim V + \dim V^\perp = n$. Every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ splits in exactly one way as (a vector in $V$) $+$ (a vector in $V^\perp$).

Example: In $\mathbb{R}^3$, the complement of a plane through the origin is the line through the origin perpendicular to the plane, and the dimensions are $2 + 1 = 3$.

Tip: To check $w \in V^\perp$ it is enough to test $w$ against a basis of $V$.
cards.searchQuery: orthogonal complement of a subspace definition

cards.title: How are the row space and the null space of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ related?
cards.body:
They are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^n$: $N(A) = C(A^T)^\perp$. Likewise, in $\mathbb{R}^m$, $N(A^T) = C(A)^\perp$.

Why: $Ax = 0$ says that every row of $A$ has dot product $0$ with $x$. So $x$ is orthogonal to each row, hence to every combination of the rows, which is the whole row space. Conversely, a vector orthogonal to all rows has $Ax = 0$.

Why it matters: The dimensions $r$ and $n - r$ add up to $n$, so the two spaces together exactly fill $\mathbb{R}^n$. Any $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the sum of a row-space part and a null-space part.

Watch out: Orthogonal means every vector of one is perpendicular to every vector of the other. The two spaces share only $0$.

cards.title: What is the **projection** $p$ of $b$ onto the line through a nonzero vector $a$, and what is its **projection matrix** $P$ (with $p = Pb$)?
cards.body:
$p = \dfrac{a^T b}{a^T a}\,a$, so $P = \dfrac{a a^T}{a^T a}$.

Why: Write $p = \hat{x}\,a$ and require the error $e = b - p$ to be orthogonal to $a$: $a^T(b - \hat{x}a) = 0$, which gives $\hat{x} = \dfrac{a^T b}{a^T a}$.

Here $a a^T$ is a matrix (a column times a row) and $a^T a$ is a number. The matrix $P$ satisfies $P^T = P$ and $P^2 = P$: projecting twice does nothing new.

Example: For $a = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ we have $a^Ta = 9$, so $P = \dfrac{1}{9}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 2\\2 & 4 & 4\\2 & 4 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
cards.searchQuery: projection onto a line formula projection matrix aa^T

cards.title: If the columns of $A$ are independent, what is the projection matrix onto the column space $C(A)$?
cards.body:
$P = A (A^T A)^{-1} A^T$, and the projection of $b$ is $p = Pb = A\hat{x}$ with $A^T A\,\hat{x} = A^T b$.

Why: The projection $p = A\hat{x}$ must be in $C(A)$, and the error $b - A\hat{x}$ must be orthogonal to every column of $A$, which says $A^T(b - A\hat{x}) = 0$. Solving gives $\hat{x} = (A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb$.

Why it matters: This extends the one-vector formula to any subspace, and it is the engine behind least squares.

Watch out: The inverse $(A^TA)^{-1}$ exists only when the columns of $A$ are independent. If $A$ is not square, $A^{-1}$ does not exist, so $(A^TA)^{-1}$ cannot be split into $A^{-1}(A^T)^{-1}$; do not cancel the factors.
cards.searchQuery: projection matrix onto column space A(A^TA)^-1 A^T

cards.title: Project $b = \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ onto the plane spanned by $u = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $w = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
cards.body:
$p = \begin{pmatrix}\tfrac23\\\tfrac23\\\tfrac43\end{pmatrix}$, with error $e = b - p = \begin{pmatrix}\tfrac13\\\tfrac13\\-\tfrac13\end{pmatrix}$.

Let $A$ have columns $u$ and $w$. Then $A^T A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $A^T b = \begin{pmatrix}2\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Solving $A^TA\,\hat{x} = A^Tb$ gives $\hat{x} = (\tfrac23, \tfrac23)$, so $p = \tfrac23 u + \tfrac23 w$.

Check: The error is orthogonal to the plane: $e \cdot u = \tfrac13 - \tfrac13 = 0$ and $e \cdot w = \tfrac13 - \tfrac13 = 0$.

Tip: This plane is $z = x + y$, whose perpendicular direction is $(1, 1, -1)$. The error is a multiple of it, as it must be.
cards.searchQuery: project vector onto plane spanned by two vectors example

cards.title: What is an **orthonormal basis**, and what does $Q^T Q = I$ say about a matrix $Q$ with orthonormal columns?
cards.body:
A basis $q_1, \dots, q_k$ with $q_i \cdot q_j = 0$ for $i \ne j$ and $q_i \cdot q_i = 1$; for the matrix $Q$ with these columns, $Q^T Q = I$.

The entries of $Q^TQ$ are exactly the dot products $q_i \cdot q_j$, so $Q^TQ = I$ restates the definition. If $Q$ is square (an **orthogonal matrix**), then $Q^{-1} = Q^T$.

Why it matters: Coordinates are free: if $v = c_1 q_1 + \dots + c_k q_k$, then $c_i = q_i \cdot v$. Also $\|Qx\| = \|x\|$, since $(Qx)^T(Qx) = x^T Q^T Q x = x^T x$: multiplying by $Q$ preserves lengths and dot products.

Example: A rotation matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\\sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$ is orthogonal.

cards.title: Apply the **Gram–Schmidt process** to $a_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $a_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and write the **QR factorization** $A = QR$ of the matrix $A$ with these columns.
cards.body:
$q_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, $q_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$, and $R = \begin{pmatrix}\sqrt2 & 1/\sqrt2\\0 & \sqrt6/2\end{pmatrix}$.

Gram–Schmidt turns independent vectors into an orthonormal list: take each vector, subtract its components along the earlier $q$'s, then divide by the length.

1. $\|a_1\| = \sqrt2$, so $q_1 = a_1/\sqrt2$.
2. $q_1 \cdot a_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$. Subtract: $a_2 - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}q_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12\\\tfrac12\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12\\-\tfrac12\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
3. Its length is $\sqrt{3/2} = \tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}$, so $q_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$.

In $A = QR$, $R$ is upper triangular with $r_{ij} = q_i \cdot a_j$, so $r_{11} = \sqrt2$, $r_{12} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $r_{22} = \tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}$.

Check: $r_{12}q_1 + r_{22}q_2 = \begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12\\\tfrac12\\0\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12\\-\tfrac12\\1\end{pmatrix} = a_2$.

cards.title: Why is it false that a matrix with mutually orthogonal columns always satisfies $Q^T Q = I$?
cards.body:
Orthogonal columns make $Q^TQ$ diagonal, but its diagonal entries are the squared lengths of the columns, which equal $1$ only if the columns are unit vectors.

Example: $Q = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$ has orthogonal columns, but $Q^T Q = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\0 & 2\end{pmatrix} = 2I$. Dividing each column by $\sqrt2$ gives a matrix that does satisfy $Q^TQ = I$.

Key idea: Orthonormal means orthogonal and of length one. The normalizing step is separate from the orthogonalizing step.

Watch out: Also, an $m \times n$ matrix with orthonormal columns satisfies $Q^TQ = I_n$ but not $QQ^T = I_m$ unless it is square.

cards.title: When $Ax = b$ has no solution, what does **least squares** choose instead, geometrically?
cards.body:
It picks $\hat{x}$ so that $A\hat{x}$ is the projection of $b$ onto the column space $C(A)$, the point of $C(A)$ closest to $b$.

The **residual** $e = b - A\hat{x}$ is what is left over, and it is orthogonal to $C(A)$. Least squares makes the length $\|e\|$ as small as possible, which is the same as making the sum of the squares of the entries of $e$ as small as possible.

Why: Every $Ax$ lies in $C(A)$, and the closest point of a subspace to $b$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $b$, that is, the projection.

Key idea: An unsolvable system means $b$ is not in $C(A)$. Least squares solves the nearest solvable system, $A\hat{x} = p$.
cards.searchQuery: least squares geometry projection onto column space residual

cards.title: State the **normal equations**: which condition characterizes a least-squares solution $\hat{x}$ of $Ax = b$, and when is it unique?
cards.body:
$\hat{x}$ minimizes $\|b - Ax\|$ if and only if $A^TA\,\hat{x} = A^Tb$; the minimizer is unique exactly when the columns of $A$ are independent.

Key idea: The residual $e = b - A\hat{x}$ is orthogonal to every column of $A$, which says $A^T e = 0$, and that is $A^TA\hat{x} = A^Tb$. For any other $x$, Pythagoras gives $\|b - Ax\|^2 = \|e\|^2 + \|A(\hat{x} - x)\|^2 \ge \|e\|^2$.

When the columns are independent, $A^TA$ is invertible and $\hat{x} = (A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb$. With dependent columns there are infinitely many minimizers, all giving the same $A\hat{x}$.

Watch out: The normal equations always have a solution, even when $Ax = b$ has none.
cards.searchQuery: normal equations A^T A x hat = A^T b least squares theorem

cards.title: For data points $(t_1, y_1), \dots, (t_m, y_m)$, what are the normal equations for the **best-fit line** $y = C + Dt$?
cards.body:
$\begin{pmatrix} m & \sum t_i \\ \sum t_i & \sum t_i^2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} C \\ D \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum y_i \\ \sum t_i y_i \end{pmatrix}$

Why: The ideal system $C + Dt_i = y_i$ is $Ax = b$ with $A$ having rows $(1, t_i)$ and $x = (C, D)$. Then $A^TA$ and $A^Tb$ are exactly the matrix and right side above.

Here "best" means the least squares sense: $C$ and $D$ make $\sum (y_i - C - Dt_i)^2$ as small as possible.

Tip: The matrix is invertible as soon as at least two of the $t_i$ differ, since the two columns of $A$ are then independent.
cards.searchQuery: best fit line normal equations sums least squares formula

cards.title: Find the best-fit line $y = C + Dt$ through the points $(0, 0)$, $(1, 3)$, $(2, 3)$.
cards.body:
$y = \tfrac12 + \tfrac32\,t$

The normal equations are $3C + 3D = 6$ (from $\sum y = 6$) and $3C + 5D = 9$ (from $\sum ty = 0 + 3 + 6 = 9$). Subtracting gives $2D = 3$, so $D = \tfrac32$ and then $C = \tfrac12$.

The line has heights $\tfrac12,\ 2,\ \tfrac72$ at $t = 0, 1, 2$, so the residual is $e = \begin{pmatrix}-\tfrac12\\1\\-\tfrac12\end{pmatrix}$.

Check: $e$ is orthogonal to both columns of $A$: $(1,1,1) \cdot e = 0$ and $(0,1,2) \cdot e = 1 - 1 = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: fit line to three points least squares example

cards.title: Show that the number $x$ minimizing $(x - b_1)^2 + \dots + (x - b_m)^2$ is the mean of $b_1, \dots, b_m$, using the normal equations.
cards.body:
The best constant is $\hat{x} = \dfrac{b_1 + \dots + b_m}{m}$, the mean of the data.

The problem is the least-squares problem for $Ax = b$ where $A$ is the single column of $m$ ones, so $Ax = b$ says "$x = b_i$ for every $i$".

1. $A^TA = 1 + \dots + 1 = m$ and $A^Tb = b_1 + \dots + b_m$.
2. The normal equation is $m\,\hat{x} = b_1 + \dots + b_m$.
3. So $\hat{x}$ is the average of the $b_i$.

Why it matters: The mean is the projection of $b$ onto the line spanned by $(1, \dots, 1)$, and the residual entries $b_i - \hat{x}$ add to $0$.

cards.title: Find the slope $D$ that minimizes $(D - 2)^2 + (2D - 3)^2 + (3D - 7)^2$. Type the exact fraction.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{29}{14}$

This is least squares for the line $y = Dt$ through the points $(1, 2)$, $(2, 3)$, $(3, 7)$, so $A$ has the single column $a = (1, 2, 3)$ and $b = (2, 3, 7)$.

1. $a^Ta = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14$ and $a^Tb = 2 + 6 + 21 = 29$.
2. The normal equation $14\,\hat{D} = 29$ gives $\hat{D} = \tfrac{29}{14}$.

Check: The residual is $e = b - \hat{D}a = (-\tfrac1{14}, -\tfrac{16}{14}, \tfrac{11}{14})$, and $a \cdot e = \tfrac{-1 - 32 + 33}{14} = 0$.

cards.title: Why is it false that the least-squares line minimizes the perpendicular distances from the data points to the line?
cards.body:
It minimizes the sum of the squares of the vertical errors $y_i - (C + Dt_i)$, measured in the $y$-direction, not the perpendicular distances.

Why: In $Ax = b$ the errors are the entries of $b - Ax$, one per data point, and each is a difference of $y$-values at the same $t_i$. This treats $t$ as known exactly and $y$ as the measured quantity.

Example: Change the units of $y$ (say, meters to centimeters). The least-squares line is the old line expressed in the new units, but the line minimizing perpendicular distances can come out as a genuinely different line, since stretching one axis changes which distances are perpendicular.

Watch out: Fitting by perpendicular distance is a different method, with a different answer. The word "normal" in "normal equations" refers to orthogonality in $\mathbb{R}^m$, not to the geometry of the scatter plot.

cards.title: What three properties define the **determinant** of an $n \times n$ matrix, including its **multilinearity**?
cards.body:
$\det I = 1$; exchanging two rows changes the sign; and $\det$ is linear in each row separately, with the other rows held fixed.

**Multilinearity** means two things for the first row (and likewise for any other): $\det$ with row 1 replaced by $t\,r$ is $t$ times $\det$ with row $r$; and $\det$ with row 1 replaced by $r + r'$ is the sum of the two determinants.

These properties force everything else. A matrix with two equal rows has $\det = 0$ (swap them: $\det = -\det$). Subtracting a multiple of one row from another leaves $\det$ unchanged. So elimination gives $\det A = \pm(\text{product of the pivots})$, with the sign from the row exchanges, and $\det A \ne 0$ exactly when $A$ is invertible.

Watch out: Linear in each row separately is not the same as $\det(A + B) = \det A + \det B$, which is false.

cards.title: State the product rule for determinants of $n \times n$ matrices $A$ and $B$, and one consequence for inverses.
cards.body:
$\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)$, so for invertible $A$, $\det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det A}$.

Why it matters: Factorizations turn into determinant calculations. From $A = LU$ with $L$ having $1$s on the diagonal, $\det A = \det U$, the product of the pivots.

The consequence follows from $\det(A)\det(A^{-1}) = \det(AA^{-1}) = \det I = 1$. Also $\det(A^T) = \det A$, so every row property also holds for columns.

Key idea (of the proof): For fixed $B$, the function $A \mapsto \det(AB)/\det B$ (when $\det B \ne 0$) has the three defining properties, so it must equal $\det A$.

Watch out: There is no such rule for sums: $\det(A + B) \ne \det A + \det B$ in general.
cards.searchQuery: determinant of product det(AB)=det A det B inverse

cards.title: What does $|\det A|$ measure for an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, geometrically?
cards.body:
The $n$-dimensional **volume** of the box (parallelepiped) whose edges are the rows of $A$; in the plane it is the area of the parallelogram.

For $n = 2$ with rows $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$, the area is $|ad - bc|$.

Why: Signed volume has the same three defining properties as the determinant. The unit cube has volume $1$; stretching one edge by $t$ multiplies volume by $t$; and sliding one edge along another (adding a multiple of a row to another) shears the box without changing its volume.

Key idea: $\det A = 0$ exactly when the box is flat, that is, when the rows are dependent. Because $\det A^T = \det A$, the columns give the same volume.
cards.searchQuery: determinant equals volume of parallelepiped rows

cards.title: What is the **cofactor expansion** of $\det A$ along row $i$ of an $n \times n$ matrix?
cards.body:
$\det A = a_{i1}C_{i1} + a_{i2}C_{i2} + \dots + a_{in}C_{in}$, where $C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$ and $M_{ij}$ is the determinant of $A$ with row $i$ and column $j$ deleted.

The number $C_{ij}$ is the **cofactor** of the entry $a_{ij}$. The signs $(-1)^{i+j}$ form a checkerboard starting with $+$ in the top left corner. The same expansion works along any row, or down any column.

Tip: Expand along a row or column with many zeros: each zero entry kills its term.

Watch out: Expanding every minor in turn takes about $n!$ operations, so for large matrices elimination is far cheaper. Use cofactors for small matrices, for symbolic entries and for proofs.
cards.searchQuery: cofactor expansion determinant formula along row

cards.title: What is the **adjugate matrix** $\operatorname{adj}(A)$, and what formula expresses $A^{-1}$ with it?
cards.body:
$A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj}(A)$, where $\operatorname{adj}(A)$ is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors, so $\operatorname{adj}(A)_{ij} = C_{ji}$.

Why: The product of row $i$ of $A$ with the cofactors of row $k$ is a cofactor expansion, so it equals $\det A$ when $i = k$ and equals $0$ otherwise (it is the determinant of a matrix with two equal rows). Hence $A\,\operatorname{adj}(A) = (\det A)\,I$.

Example: For a $2 \times 2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a & b\\c & d\end{pmatrix}$ the cofactors give $\operatorname{adj}(A) = \begin{pmatrix}d & -b\\-c & a\end{pmatrix}$, so $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix}d & -b\\-c & a\end{pmatrix}$.

Watch out: Note the transpose: the $(i, j)$ entry of $A^{-1}$ uses the cofactor $C_{ji}$, with the indices reversed.
cards.searchQuery: adjugate matrix inverse formula cofactors transpose

cards.title: Use **Cramer's rule** to solve $2x + y = 5$, $x + 3y = 5$.
cards.body:
$(x, y) = (2, 1)$

Cramer's rule says that for an invertible $A$, the solution of $Ax = b$ has $x_j = \dfrac{\det B_j}{\det A}$, where $B_j$ is $A$ with column $j$ replaced by $b$.

Here $\det A = 2\cdot 3 - 1\cdot 1 = 5$. With column 1 replaced by $b$: $\det \begin{pmatrix}5 & 1\\5 & 3\end{pmatrix} = 15 - 5 = 10$, so $x = 10/5 = 2$. With column 2 replaced: $\det \begin{pmatrix}2 & 5\\1 & 5\end{pmatrix} = 10 - 5 = 5$, so $y = 5/5 = 1$.

Why it works: $x = A^{-1}b = \frac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj}(A)\,b$, and the $j$th entry of $\operatorname{adj}(A)\,b$ is a cofactor expansion of $\det B_j$.

Watch out: Cramer's rule is elegant but slow. For numerical solving, use elimination.
cards.searchQuery: Cramer's rule 2x2 example solve system determinants

cards.title: Compute $\det A$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 2 & 1\\1 & 1 & 2\\2 & 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ by elimination.
cards.body:
$\det A = 5$

1. The first pivot position holds $0$, so exchange rows 1 and 2. One exchange flips the sign: keep a factor $-1$.
2. The matrix is now $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\\0 & 2 & 1\\2 & 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Subtract $2\times$ row 1 from row 3: the row becomes $(0,-1,-3)$.
3. Add $\tfrac12\times$ row 2 to row 3: the row becomes $(0,0,-\tfrac52)$. The pivots are $1, 2, -\tfrac52$.
4. $\det A = (-1)\cdot 1 \cdot 2 \cdot (-\tfrac52) = 5$.

Check: Expanding along row 1 gives $0 - 2\cdot(1\cdot 1 - 2\cdot 2) + 1\cdot(1\cdot 1 - 1\cdot 2) = 6 - 1 = 5$.

cards.title: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & 0\\1 & 3 & 1\\0 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, use cofactors to find the entry in row 1, column 2 of $A^{-1}$. Type the exact fraction.
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{1}{4}$

1. Expanding along row 1: $\det A = 2(3\cdot 2 - 1\cdot 1) - 1(1\cdot 2 - 1\cdot 0) + 0 = 10 - 2 = 8$.
2. The entry $(A^{-1})_{12}$ uses $C_{21}$ (indices reversed). Delete row 2 and column 1 to get $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $2$, so $C_{21} = (-1)^{2+1}\cdot 2 = -2$.
3. $(A^{-1})_{12} = \dfrac{C_{21}}{\det A} = \dfrac{-2}{8} = -\dfrac14$.

Check: Row 1 of $A$ against column 2 of $A^{-1}$ must give $0$. That column is $(-\tfrac14, \tfrac12, -\tfrac14)$, and $2(-\tfrac14) + 1(\tfrac12) + 0 = 0$.

cards.title: Why is it false that $\det(2A) = 2\det(A)$ for a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$?
cards.body:
Multiplying the whole matrix by $2$ scales all $3$ rows, each contributing a factor $2$, so $\det(2A) = 2^3 \det A = 8\det A$.

In general $\det(cA) = c^n \det A$ for an $n \times n$ matrix. Linearity applies to one row at a time, and $cA$ has $n$ rows to scale.

Example: $A = I$ ($3 \times 3$) has $\det A = 1$, and $2I$ is diagonal with entries $2, 2, 2$, so $\det(2I) = 8$.

Geometric view: Doubling every edge of a box multiplies its volume by $2^3 = 8$, not by $2$.
cards.searchQuery: determinant of scalar multiple det(cA)=c^n det A

cards.title: What are an **eigenvalue** and an **eigenvector** of a square matrix $A$?
cards.body:
A nonzero vector $x$ with $Ax = \lambda x$ is an eigenvector, and the number $\lambda$ is its eigenvalue.

An eigenvector is a direction that $A$ does not turn: it only stretches it by $\lambda$ (and flips it if $\lambda < 0$). Equivalently, $(A - \lambda I)x = 0$ with $x \ne 0$, so $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $A - \lambda I$ is singular.

Example: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\0 & 5\end{pmatrix}$, the vector $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ has $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix} = 2\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, so $2$ is an eigenvalue. The vector $\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ goes with the eigenvalue $5$.

Watch out: The zero vector is excluded by definition, since $A \cdot 0 = \lambda \cdot 0$ for every $\lambda$. The eigenvalue $0$ is allowed, and it occurs exactly when $A$ is singular.
cards.searchQuery: eigenvalue eigenvector definition Ax = lambda x

cards.title: What is the **characteristic polynomial** of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, and what are its roots?
cards.body:
$p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$, a polynomial of degree $n$ whose roots are exactly the eigenvalues of $A$.

Why: $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue when $A - \lambda I$ is singular, and a matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is $0$. A root that appears $m$ times has **algebraic multiplicity** $m$. Over $\mathbb{C}$ there are always $n$ roots counted this way (the fundamental theorem of algebra).

For $2 \times 2$: $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - (\operatorname{trace} A)\lambda + \det A$, where the trace is the sum of the diagonal entries.

Watch out: A real matrix can have complex eigenvalues. The rotation $\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ has $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 + 1$ and eigenvalues $\pm i$.
cards.searchQuery: characteristic polynomial det(A - lambda I) eigenvalues roots

cards.title: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1\\2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.
cards.body:
Eigenvalues $5$ and $2$, with eigenvectors $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$.

The characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 2)$.

For $\lambda = 5$: $A - 5I = \begin{pmatrix}-1 & 1\\2 & -2\end{pmatrix}$, whose null space is spanned by $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. For $\lambda = 2$: $A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, whose null space is spanned by $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$.

Check: $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4-2\\\ 2-6\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-4\end{pmatrix} = 2\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$. Also the trace is $4 + 3 = 7 = 5 + 2$ and the determinant is $12 - 2 = 10 = 5 \cdot 2$.

Tip: After finding $\lambda$, the rows of $A - \lambda I$ must be dependent. If they are not, the arithmetic is off.
cards.searchQuery: eigenvalues eigenvectors 2x2 matrix example characteristic polynomial

cards.title: How are the trace and the determinant of an $n \times n$ matrix related to its eigenvalues?
cards.body:
With eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ counted by algebraic multiplicity (over $\mathbb{C}$): $\operatorname{trace} A = \lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_n$ and $\det A = \lambda_1 \lambda_2 \cdots \lambda_n$.

Why: The characteristic polynomial factors as $\det(A - \lambda I) = (\lambda_1 - \lambda)\cdots(\lambda_n - \lambda)$. Setting $\lambda = 0$ gives $\det A = \lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n$. The coefficient of $\lambda^{n-1}$ is, on the left, $(-1)^{n-1}\operatorname{trace} A$ and, on the right, $(-1)^{n-1}(\lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_n)$.

Why it matters: A fast check on every eigenvalue computation, and it shows that $A$ is singular exactly when some eigenvalue is $0$.

Example: A $2 \times 2$ matrix with trace $2$ and determinant $-3$ has characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 3 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 1)$, so its eigenvalues are $3$ and $-1$.
cards.searchQuery: trace sum of eigenvalues determinant product of eigenvalues

cards.title: What can you say about eigenvectors that belong to different eigenvalues, and what does it give for a matrix with $n$ distinct eigenvalues?
cards.body:
Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so an $n \times n$ matrix with $n$ distinct eigenvalues has $n$ independent eigenvectors.

Key idea (two eigenvectors): Suppose $c_1x_1 + c_2x_2 = 0$ with $Ax_i = \lambda_i x_i$ and $\lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2$. Apply $A$: $c_1\lambda_1 x_1 + c_2\lambda_2 x_2 = 0$. Subtract $\lambda_2$ times the first equation: $c_1(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)x_1 = 0$. Since $x_1 \ne 0$ and $\lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2$, $c_1 = 0$, and then $c_2 = 0$.

Why it matters: Distinct eigenvalues are a quick sufficient condition for diagonalizability.

Watch out: The converse is false: the identity matrix has the single eigenvalue $1$ yet has $n$ independent eigenvectors.
cards.searchQuery: eigenvectors distinct eigenvalues linearly independent theorem

cards.title: If $A$ has $n$ independent eigenvectors, which factorization is its **diagonalization**, and what is $A^k$?
cards.body:
$A = X\Lambda X^{-1}$, where the columns of $X$ are $n$ independent eigenvectors and $\Lambda$ is diagonal with the matching eigenvalues; then $A^k = X\Lambda^k X^{-1}$.

Why: The $n$ equations $Ax_i = \lambda_i x_i$ say $AX = X\Lambda$. The matrix $X$ is invertible because its columns are independent, so $A = X\Lambda X^{-1}$.

Why it matters: In $A^k = X\Lambda X^{-1}X\Lambda X^{-1}\cdots$ the middle factors cancel, and $\Lambda^k$ just raises each diagonal entry to the $k$th power.

Watch out: The columns of $X$ and the entries of $\Lambda$ must be in the same order. Not every matrix can be diagonalized: the factorization exists exactly when there are $n$ independent eigenvectors.
cards.searchQuery: diagonalization A = X Lambda X inverse powers of matrix

cards.title: Give a $2 \times 2$ matrix that cannot be diagonalized, and say why.
cards.body:
$A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$: the eigenvalue $1$ appears twice, but every eigenvector is a multiple of $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, so there is no second independent eigenvector.

The characteristic polynomial is $(1 - \lambda)^2$, so $\lambda = 1$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$. But $A - I = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ has null space spanned by $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ alone, so the **geometric multiplicity** (the dimension of $N(A - \lambda I)$) is $1$.

Why: A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when, for every eigenvalue, the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity. Here $1 < 2$: too few eigenvectors to form $X$.

Key idea: This matrix shears the plane, pushing points sideways in proportion to their height. A shear leaves only one direction unchanged.
cards.searchQuery: non-diagonalizable matrix shear geometric algebraic multiplicity

cards.title: Why is it false that a matrix with a repeated eigenvalue cannot be diagonalized?
cards.body:
Repeated eigenvalues are harmless if there are still enough independent eigenvectors; what matters is the number of eigenvectors, not whether the eigenvalues repeat.

Example: The $2 \times 2$ identity matrix has the eigenvalue $1$ twice, and every nonzero vector is an eigenvector, so $X = I$ works and $I = I\cdot I\cdot I^{-1}$ is already diagonal.

Key idea: Diagonalizable means geometric multiplicity equals algebraic multiplicity for each eigenvalue. Repetition only creates the possibility of failure, as with $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.

Tip: Distinct eigenvalues guarantee diagonalizability, but diagonalizability does not require distinct eigenvalues.
cards.searchQuery: repeated eigenvalue still diagonalizable identity matrix

cards.title: Use diagonalization to find a formula for $A^k$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1\\2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.
cards.body:
$A^k = \dfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2\cdot 5^k + 2^k & \ 5^k - 2^k\\\ 2\cdot 5^k - 2\cdot 2^k & \ 5^k + 2\cdot 2^k\end{pmatrix}$

1. From the example, $X = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & -2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\Lambda = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 0\\0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$.
2. $\det X = -3$, so $X^{-1} = \tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$.
3. $X\Lambda^k = \begin{pmatrix}5^k & 2^k\\5^k & -2\cdot 2^k\end{pmatrix}$, and multiplying by $X^{-1}$ gives the matrix above.

Check: $k = 1$ gives $\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}12 & 3\\6 & 9\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1\\2 & 3\end{pmatrix} = A$, and $k = 0$ gives $I$.
cards.searchQuery: matrix power formula via diagonalization 2x2 example

cards.title: A **Markov matrix** has nonnegative entries and each column adding to $1$. For $A = \begin{pmatrix}0.9 & 0.2\\0.1 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}$, find its eigenvalues and the steady state, the eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$ whose entries add to $1$.
cards.body:
The eigenvalues are $1$ and $0.7$, and the steady state is $(\tfrac23, \tfrac13)$.

1. Every Markov matrix has the eigenvalue $1$: the columns of $A$ add to $1$, so the rows of $A - I$ add to the zero row and $A - I$ is singular. The trace is $1.7$, so the other eigenvalue is $0.7$.
2. $A - I = \begin{pmatrix}-0.1 & 0.2\\0.1 & -0.2\end{pmatrix}$ has null space spanned by $\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Rescale so the entries add to $1$: $(\tfrac23, \tfrac13)$.

Why it matters: For any starting vector $u_0$ with entries adding to $1$, $A^k u_0 = c_1 (1)^k x_1 + c_2 (0.7)^k x_2 \to c_1 x_1$ as $k \to \infty$. The $0.7^k$ part dies out, and the sum of entries stays $1$, so the limit is the steady state.

Check: $0.9\cdot\tfrac23 + 0.2\cdot\tfrac13 = \tfrac23$ and $0.1\cdot\tfrac23 + 0.8\cdot\tfrac13 = \tfrac13$, so $A$ leaves the vector unchanged.
cards.searchQuery: Markov matrix steady state eigenvector eigenvalue one

cards.title: State the **spectral theorem** for a real symmetric $n \times n$ matrix $A$.
cards.body:
All eigenvalues of $A$ are real, and $\mathbb{R}^n$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of $A$; so $A = Q\Lambda Q^T$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $\Lambda$ real diagonal.

Why: Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are already orthogonal. If $Ax_1 = \lambda_1 x_1$ and $Ax_2 = \lambda_2 x_2$, then $\lambda_1\, x_1 \cdot x_2 = (Ax_1) \cdot x_2 = x_1 \cdot (Ax_2) = \lambda_2\, x_1 \cdot x_2$ (using $A^T = A$), so $x_1 \cdot x_2 = 0$ when $\lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2$.

This is why symmetric matrices are the best-behaved matrices: they are always diagonalizable, with $X = Q$ and $X^{-1} = Q^T$.

Watch out: The statement needs $A$ real and symmetric. A real non-symmetric matrix can have complex eigenvalues, and the theorem says nothing about it.
cards.searchQuery: spectral theorem real symmetric matrix orthonormal eigenvectors

cards.title: What does **orthogonal diagonalization** $A = Q\Lambda Q^T$ say about how a symmetric matrix $A$ acts on a vector $x$?
cards.body:
$A$ splits $x$ into its components along the orthonormal eigenvectors $q_i$, scales the $i$th component by $\lambda_i$, and puts the pieces back together: $Ax = \sum_i \lambda_i (q_i \cdot x)\,q_i$.

In matrix form $A = \lambda_1 q_1q_1^T + \dots + \lambda_n q_nq_n^T$. Each $q_iq_i^T$ is the projection matrix onto the line through $q_i$, so $A$ is a weighted sum of projections onto perpendicular lines.

Key idea: In the right coordinate system, which is the system of the $q_i$, a symmetric matrix is just $n$ separate scalings with no mixing. Because $Q$ is orthogonal, changing coordinates does not distort lengths or angles.
cards.searchQuery: orthogonal diagonalization symmetric matrix sum of projections

cards.title: What is a **positive definite matrix**?
cards.body:
A real symmetric matrix $A$ with $x^T A x > 0$ for every nonzero vector $x$.

The number $x^TAx$ is a quadratic expression in the entries of $x$. For $A = \begin{pmatrix}a & b\\b & c\end{pmatrix}$ it is $ax_1^2 + 2bx_1x_2 + cx_2^2$. Positive definite matrices are the matrices for which this expression is a "bowl" with its minimum at $x = 0$.

Example: $I$ is positive definite, since $x^TIx = x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2 > 0$ for $x \ne 0$.

Watch out: The condition is strict and applies to every nonzero $x$. If $x^TAx \ge 0$ is all you can guarantee, the matrix is only positive semidefinite.
cards.searchQuery: positive definite matrix definition x^T A x > 0

cards.title: For a real symmetric matrix $A$, which four conditions are equivalent to $A$ being positive definite?
cards.body:
All eigenvalues are positive; elimination (without row exchanges) gives $n$ positive pivots; the $n$ leading determinants are positive; and $x^TAx > 0$ for all $x \ne 0$ (the definition itself, listed as the fourth test).

The **leading determinants** are the determinants of the upper-left $1 \times 1$, $2 \times 2$, ..., $n \times n$ blocks of $A$.

Why: In terms of the spectral theorem, $x^TAx = \lambda_1 c_1^2 + \dots + \lambda_n c_n^2$ where $c_i = q_i \cdot x$, which is positive for all $x \ne 0$ exactly when every $\lambda_i > 0$. The $k$th leading determinant equals the product of the first $k$ pivots, so all pivots are positive exactly when all leading determinants are.

Tip: For a quick test of a $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix, check that $a > 0$ and $ac - b^2 > 0$.
cards.searchQuery: positive definite tests eigenvalues pivots leading determinants

cards.title: Show that $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\-1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ is positive definite using each of the four tests.
cards.body:
All four tests pass: eigenvalues $1$ and $3$, pivots $2$ and $\tfrac32$, leading determinants $2$ and $3$, and $x^TAx > 0$.

- Eigenvalues: $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 3)$, so $1$ and $3$.
- Pivots: the first is $2$; subtracting $-\tfrac12$ times row 1 from row 2 leaves $2 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac32$.
- Leading determinants: $2$ and $4 - 1 = 3$.
- Quadratic form: $x^TAx = 2x_1^2 - 2x_1x_2 + 2x_2^2 = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + (x_1 - x_2)^2$, a sum of squares that vanishes only at $x = 0$.

Check: The product of the pivots, $2 \cdot \tfrac32 = 3$, equals the determinant and equals the product of the eigenvalues, $1 \cdot 3$.

cards.title: Why is it false that a symmetric matrix with all positive entries is positive definite?
cards.body:
Positive entries do not control the sign of $x^TAx$; the eigenvalues or pivots do, and a matrix with all positive entries can still have a negative eigenvalue.

Example: $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has $x^TAx = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + x_2^2$, which at $x = (1,-1)$ equals $1 - 4 + 1 = -2 < 0$. Its eigenvalues are $3$ and $-1$, and the second pivot is $1 - 4 = -3$.

Key idea: Large off-diagonal entries relative to the diagonal ones are what spoil positive definiteness. In the $2 \times 2$ case the test is $a > 0$ and $ac > b^2$.

Watch out: The converse also fails: $\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\-1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ is positive definite and has negative entries.
cards.searchQuery: positive entries not enough positive definite counterexample

cards.title: What is the **singular value decomposition** of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ of rank $r$, and what are its **singular values**?
cards.body:
$A = U\Sigma V^T$ with $U$ ($m \times m$) and $V$ ($n \times n$) orthogonal and $\Sigma$ ($m \times n$) zero except for the singular values $\sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_r > 0$ on its diagonal; $\sigma_i^2$ are the nonzero eigenvalues of $A^TA$.

The columns of $V$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A^TA$, the columns of $U$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $AA^T$, and $Av_i = \sigma_i u_i$. The **singular values** are $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i(A^TA)}$.

Why it matters: Every matrix, square or not, has one. Geometrically, $A$ rotates (by $V^T$), stretches along the axes by the $\sigma_i$ (by $\Sigma$) and rotates again (by $U$).

Watch out: Singular values are never negative, and they are not the eigenvalues of $A$ unless $A$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
cards.searchQuery: singular value decomposition A = U Sigma V transpose singular values

cards.title: Find the singular values of $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 0\\4 & 5\end{pmatrix}$.
cards.body:
$\sigma_1 = 3\sqrt5$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt5$.

1. $A^TA = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 4\\0 & 5\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3 & 0\\4 & 5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}25 & 20\\20 & 25\end{pmatrix}$.
2. Its characteristic polynomial is $(25 - \lambda)^2 - 400$, so $\lambda = 25 \pm 20$, that is $45$ and $5$.
3. The singular values are the square roots: $\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt5$ and $\sqrt5$.

Check: $\sigma_1\sigma_2 = 15 = |\det A|$, and $\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 = 50 = 3^2 + 0^2 + 4^2 + 5^2$, the sum of the squares of all entries (which equals $\operatorname{trace}(A^TA)$).
